title: Battle of Bar
description: Stefan Vojislav of Duklja destroys a Byzantine army in the mountains and secures his state's independence.

title: Mihailo recognised as king
description: Pope Gregory VII addresses Mihailo of Duklja as king, the first royal title in these lands.

title: Cetinje founded
description: Ivan Crnojević, driven from the plain by the Ottomans, moves his court to a field under Mount Lovćen and builds a monastery there.

title: Crnojević printing house
description: The monk Makarije prints the Oktoih, the first book printed in Cyrillic among the South Slavs.

title: Ottomans take Zeta
description: The last Crnojević lord flees to Venice and the land comes under the sultan, though the mountain clans are never fully subdued.

title: Rule of the bishops begins
description: Authority passes to the bishops of Cetinje, who lead the clans for more than three centuries.

title: Danilo I elected bishop
description: Danilo Petrović-Njegoš founds the line of bishops, passing from uncle to nephew, that rules until 1918.

title: Battle of Krusi
description: The clans under Bishop Petar I defeat and kill the pasha of Scutari, and the highland tribes join Montenegro.

title: The Mountain Wreath
description: Bishop Petar II Petrović-Njegoš publishes the verse drama that becomes the central work of Montenegrin and Serbian literature.

title: Principality proclaimed
description: Danilo I gives up the office of bishop and rules as a secular prince.

title: Battle of Grahovac
description: A victory over an Ottoman army leads the powers to mark out Montenegro's border for the first time.

title: Battle of Vučji Do
description: Montenegrin and Herzegovinian fighters rout an Ottoman army in the war that leads to independence.

title: Independence recognised
description: The Treaty of Berlin recognises Montenegro as independent and doubles its territory, with an outlet to the sea at Bar.

title: Kingdom proclaimed
description: Prince Nikola takes the title of king on the fiftieth anniversary of his reign.

title: Montenegro opens the First Balkan War
description: Montenegro declares war on the Ottoman Empire ahead of its allies Serbia, Bulgaria and Greece.

title: Fall of Scutari
description: The city surrenders after a costly siege of six months, but the great powers make Montenegro hand it to the new Albania.

title: Battle of Mojkovac
description: The Montenegrin army holds the Austro-Hungarians long enough to cover the Serbian retreat, days before the kingdom surrenders.

title: Podgorica Assembly
description: An assembly deposes King Nikola and votes to unite Montenegro with Serbia.

title: Christmas Uprising
polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes
description: Supporters of the king and of a separate Montenegro rise against the union and are put down.

title: Uprising of 13 July
description: A rising against the Italian occupation frees most of the country within days, one of the first mass revolts in occupied Europe.

title: Titograd becomes the capital
description: Podgorica, flattened by bombing, is renamed after Tito and replaces Cetinje as capital of the republic.

title: Earthquake of 1979
description: An earthquake wrecks the old towns of the coast and kills over a hundred people.

title: Leadership falls to protests
description: Street protests backed by Slobodan Milošević force the republic's leaders to resign and bring his allies to power.

title: Vote to stay in Yugoslavia
description: As the federation breaks up, voters choose to stay in a common state with Serbia.

title: Đukanović elected president
description: Milo Đukanović narrowly defeats an ally of Milošević and begins to steer the republic away from Belgrade.

title: Independence referendum
description: With 55.5% in favour, just over the threshold of 55%, voters choose to leave the union with Serbia.

title: Independence declared
description: Parliament declares Montenegro independent, 88 years after it lost its statehood.

title: Montenegro joins NATO
description: Montenegro becomes the 29th member of the alliance that bombed it in 1999.
